subsection: 9. Practical application of two methods of preservation

notes.h: Home freezing: suitable foods and the principle
notes.b: Home freezing keeps food by cold, and it works best on fresh, good-quality food frozen soon after it is harvested or bought. Freezing does not improve food, so poor food comes out poor.
points: Vegetables that freeze well include carrots, peas, beans and broccoli, and fruit that freezes well includes apples and strawberries.
Meat and fish, baked foods, soups, sauces and complete meals can all be frozen at home, so a cook can store prepared dishes as well as raw ingredients.
Bananas and lettuce do not freeze well and are not suitable for home freezing, because they turn soft and limp when thawed.
Melons and pears also freeze poorly.

The principle is low temperature: freezing stops enzyme action and microbial growth (the enzymes and micro-organisms are inactivated), and the water in the food turns to ice, which micro-organisms cannot use.
Quick freezing makes small ice crystals that protect the texture of the food, whereas slow freezing makes the food softer.
notes.tip: Marks are given separately for the method name, suitable foods, steps, packaging and the principle, so give each its own paragraph. Home methods only: commercial canning or irradiation does not answer a home preservation question.

notes.h: Home freezing: preparing and blanching vegetables
notes.b: Vegetables contain enzymes that keep working in the freezer and spoil colour, flavour and texture. Blanching (a short scald in boiling water) inactivates these enzymes, so it is a key step for vegetables.
points: 1. Choose fresh, young vegetables, then wash them and prepare them by trimming, peeling and cutting them into even pieces so they blanch evenly.
2. Blanch by plunging the pieces into boiling water for the recommended time for that vegetable.
3. Cool quickly by transferring the pieces to ice-cold water for the same time as the blanching, which stops the cooking at once.
4. Drain thoroughly and dry the pieces on absorbent paper or a clean tea towel, so that surface water does not form ice.
notes.tip: Blanching is for vegetables only. Fruit is not blanched, and strawberries are open frozen instead.

notes.b: Fruit such as strawberries is frozen without blanching. The aim is to keep the pieces separate and whole.
points: Select sound, ripe fruit, wash it quickly, hull it (remove the stalk and green top) and dry it.
Open-freeze the fruit by spreading it in a single layer on a tray, so the pieces do not stick together, then pack it in portions.

notes.b: Good packing stops the food drying out and picking up flavours in the freezer, and makes it easy to use later.
points: 1. Cool cooked food completely before packing, because warm food raises the temperature of the freezer.
2. Open-freeze fruit such as strawberries by spreading them in a single layer on a tray, so the pieces do not stick together.

3. Pack the food in usable, family-sized portions in strong, moisture- and vapour-proof freezer bags or rigid containers (rigid plastic containers with tight lids, or foil), so that only what is needed is thawed.
4. Leave headspace in rigid containers, because liquids expand on freezing.
5. Remove the air from bags and seal them securely with ties or heat sealing.
6. Label each pack with its contents, quantity and the date.
notes.tip: Name the packaging in full when asked: moisture-proof and vapour-proof, air removed, sealed tightly and labelled with contents and date.

notes.b: Food must freeze quickly and then stay cold. Two different temperatures matter: the fast-freeze figure and the storage figure.
points: Switch the freezer to its fast-freeze setting 3–4 hours before adding food, so the freezer is as cold as possible when the food goes in.
Add no more than one-tenth of the freezer's capacity in any 24-hour period, because a large load of warm food raises the temperature and slows freezing.
Place new packs against the cold surfaces or in the fast-freeze section of the freezer so that they freeze quickly.
Fast freezing takes food down to about −25 °C, so it freezes quickly.
Store the frozen food at −18 °C or colder.
Rotate stock so older packs are used first, thaw food safely in the fridge, cook it thoroughly, and do not refreeze thawed raw food.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the two figures: −25 °C is fast freezing and −18 °C is storage.

notes.h: Home freezing: effect on the food
notes.b: Freezing is one of the best methods for keeping the quality of food close to the fresh product.
points: Colour, flavour, texture and nutrients are well kept when food is frozen quickly.
Some vitamin C and B1 are lost in blanching and in drip when the food thaws.
Slow freezing softens the food, because large ice crystals damage its structure.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the effect on the food alongside the method, so say what is kept and what is lost.

notes.b: Preparing food for the freezer involves sharp tools, boiling water and electrical appliances, so safe habits protect both the cook and the food.
points: Use knives, graters and food processors carefully, cutting away from the body, using the guard on the grater and keeping fingers clear of the blades, so that cuts are avoided.
Wash hands before preparation, cover any cuts with a dressing, and tie back long hair, so that bacteria and hair do not get into the food.
Use oven gloves when handling the blanching pan, turn pan handles inward, and do not overfill the pan, so that nobody is scalded.
Avoid overloaded sockets, trailing flexes and wet hands near electrical appliances, to prevent electric shock and fire.
Keep raw and cooked foods separate during preparation and clean surfaces between tasks, to prevent cross-contamination.
notes.tip: When asked for four safety guidelines, give four distinct ones and say how each prevents an accident or contamination.

notes.b: Jam keeps because several things work together: heat, sugar, pectin and acid, and a tight seal.
points: Heat at about 100 °C destroys micro-organisms and enzymes in the fruit.
Sugar preserves by osmosis: it draws water out of any micro-organism, so they cannot grow.
Pectin (a natural setting substance in fruit) and acid make the jam set.
Sealing the jar while hot prevents micro-organisms from getting back in.
notes.tip: Higher Level answers give the underlying principle, so name heat, sugar by osmosis, pectin and acid, and sealing.

notes.h: Home jam making: suitable fruit and ingredients
notes.b: Jam is made from fruit that is plentiful. Whether it sets depends mainly on how much pectin and acid the fruit contains.
points: Use ripe or just ripe, sound fruit that is free from mould and bruising, such as strawberries, raspberries, blackcurrants, plums, gooseberries, apples and blackberries.
Pectin is found mainly in the skin and core of fruit; cooking apples, blackcurrants and citrus fruit are high in pectin.
Strawberries are low in pectin, so lemon juice or another acid is added to help the jam set, and if needed pectin or pectin-rich fruit such as apple.
Sugar is added in the proportion given in a tested recipe and stirred until fully dissolved before the mixture is boiled, because undissolved sugar makes the jam crystallise.

notes.b: The steps must be in order, and each one has a purpose: sterile jars, soft fruit, dissolved sugar and a fast boil to setting point.
points: 1. Wash the jars and lids and sterilise them (in the oven or in boiling water), and keep them hot until filling, so that hot jam does not crack cold glass. Put a saucer in the freezer for the setting test and weigh the fruit and sugar.
2. Wash the fruit, remove stalks and damaged parts, and cut the fruit as the recipe requires.
3. Simmer the fruit gently in a heavy-based pan, with a little water, until it softens and releases its pectin.
4. Add the sugar and stir until it has completely dissolved, adding lemon juice if needed.
5. Bring to a full rolling boil and boil rapidly until setting point is reached; do not stir after setting point is reached.
6. Test for setting point with a cold saucer, pushing a drop of jam with a finger to check whether it wrinkles, or with a sugar thermometer at about 105 °C.
7. Take the pan off the heat and skim off the scum from the surface with a clean, dry spoon, then allow to cool slightly so the fruit does not float.
8. Pour the jam into the hot sterilised jars, leave a small space at the top, and wipe the rim.
notes.tip: Sterilise the jars and keep them hot; do not wash them and then fill them cold with hot jam. Sugar must be fully dissolved before boiling.

notes.h: Home jam making: packaging and storage
notes.b: Packaging for jam has two jobs: keeping micro-organisms out and keeping the jam in good condition.
points: Use clean, undamaged glass jars with new lids (waxed disc and cover, or twist-top lids), and wipe the rim of each jar before sealing.
Seal each jar immediately while the jam is hot, so that a vacuum forms as it cools.
Label each jar with the name of the contents and the date.
Store sealed jars in a cool, dry, dark place, and refrigerate any jar once it has been opened.

notes.h: Home jam making: faults and causes
notes.b: A jam that goes wrong can be traced back to a step that was missed.
points: Failure to set is caused by too little pectin, acid or sugar, or by not boiling long enough.
Crystallised jam is caused by too much sugar or sugar that was not dissolved.
Mould or fermentation is caused by too little sugar, unsterile jars or a poor seal.
Fruit floating is caused by potting the jam when too hot.
Scorching is caused by not stirring or by a pan that is too thin.

notes.b: Boiling jam is very hot and sticky, so most safety guidelines are about preventing burns.
points: Hot sugar syrup can cause severe scalds, so do not touch it, and handle the pan with oven gloves and pour carefully from a jug or jam funnel.
Turn pan handles inward and do not overfill the pan, as the mixture foams up and boils over when it is at a rolling boil.
Keep children and pets away from the cooker while the jam is boiling.
Remove scum with a clean, dry spoon, because a wet or used spoon can introduce micro-organisms into the jam.
Use sterilised equipment for food safety.

notes.b: A second method does not have to be jam. Chutney is an alternative, and a student may name other home methods briefly.
points: Chutney is made from foods such as apples, tomatoes, plums, onions and marrow, and heat destroys organisms while vinegar (acid) and sugar inhibit growth.

Steps: sterilise jars; chop the fruit and vegetables; cook slowly with vinegar, sugar and spices until thick; pot hot; seal with vinegar-proof lids; label; mature in a cool, dark place; refrigerate after opening. Safety is as for jam.
Chutney is boiled with vinegar and sugar and does not need pectin, whereas jam needs pectin.
Other home methods include drying herbs, apples or tomatoes (oven or dehydrator), bottling fruit and pickling vegetables in vinegar.
notes.tip: Give a full account of two home methods, preferably of different types, for example one low temperature (freezing) and one heat plus sugar (jam).

keyTerms.definition: Plunging vegetables into boiling water for a short time to inactivate enzymes before freezing, then cooling them quickly in ice-cold water.
Freezing food in a single layer on a tray before packing, so the pieces do not stick together.
The empty space left at the top of a container so that liquid can expand on freezing without breaking the container.
Using the freezer's fast-freeze setting to freeze food quickly so that small ice crystals form.
A natural substance in fruit that forms a gel with sugar and acid to set jam.
The stage in boiling jam at which enough water has evaporated and the mixture forms a gel when cooled.
Removing the scum that rises to the surface of jam during boiling.
To destroy micro-organisms on equipment, such as jars and lids, by boiling or heating them.

factCards.term: Temperature for fast-freezing food at home
factCards.definition: About -25°C, which freezes food quickly so that small ice crystals form.
Boil them in water, cool them in ice-cold water for the same time, then drain and dry them.

factCards.term: Four guidelines for freezing fresh food
factCards.definition: Cool the food first; freeze no more than one-tenth of the freezer capacity in 24 hours; use airtight, labelled packaging with the air removed; allow room for liquids to expand.
The pieces stay separate, so they can be packed in usable portions, and they freeze quickly in a single layer.
Fruit, sugar and an acid such as lemon juice.
The cold saucer test and the sugar thermometer test.
Cooking apples, blackcurrants and citrus fruit.

questions.prompt: Explain why vegetables are blanched and then plunged into ice-cold water before they are packed for the freezer.
questions.model: Blanching heats the vegetables in boiling water to inactivate enzymes, which would otherwise cause loss of colour, flavour, texture and nutrients during frozen storage. Plunging them into ice-cold water for the same time stops the cooking, so the vegetables stay firm and do not become overcooked. Drying them removes surface water, which would otherwise form ice and encourage the growth of micro-organisms.

questions.prompt: Describe a home-made preserve from fruit, from choosing the ingredients to storing the finished product, with the safety precautions at each stage.
questions.model: Ingredients: ripe, sound fruit; for a low-pectin fruit such as strawberries, lemon juice or another acid is added; sugar in the correct proportion. Preparation: wash and sterilise jars and lids and keep them hot; wash and prepare the fruit. Cooking: simmer the fruit gently in a heavy-based pan to soften it and release pectin; add the warmed sugar and stir until dissolved; boil rapidly to setting point, tested with a cold saucer or sugar thermometer. Safety: use oven gloves, turn pan handles inward, do not overfill the pan, keep children away from the cooker and handle hot syrup carefully. Finishing: skim the scum with a clean, dry spoon, pour into hot jars leaving a small space at the top, wipe the rim, and seal immediately so a vacuum forms as the jar cools. Storage: label with contents and date and store in a cool, dry, dark place; refrigerate once opened and discard any jar with a bulging lid, gas, mould or off-odour.
